subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 7. In this unit you will take your understanding of fractions to a genuinely advanced level. You already know what a fraction is and how to find simple equivalent fractions, so now we build on that foundation to master all four operations — adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing — with fractions, mixed numbers and even negative fractions. You will also learn to find fractions of amounts, and to move confidently between fractions, decimals and percentages, which are simply three different languages for the same idea.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Estimate and multiply an integer by a mixed number, and divide an integer by a proper fraction.
Estimate and subtract mixed numbers, and write the answer as a mixed number in its simplest form.
Use knowledge of the laws of arithmetic and order of operations (including brackets) to simplify calculations containing decimals or fractions.
Recognise fractions that are equivalent to recurring decimals.
Understand the relative size of quantities to compare and order decimals and fractions (positive and negative), using the symbols =, ≠, >, <, ≤ and ≥.
Estimate and multiply decimals by integers and decimals.

outcomes: Interpret a fraction as a part of a whole, a ratio, and a division, and convert freely between improper fractions and mixed numbers.
Find equivalent fractions and simplify to lowest terms using the highest common factor.
Compare and order fractions (including negative fractions) using common denominators, cross multiplication and decimals.
Add and subtract fractions and mixed numbers with unlike denominators, including borrowing.
Multiply fractions and mixed numbers, using cross-cancelling to simplify.
Divide fractions and mixed numbers using the multiply-by-the-reciprocal method.
Apply the correct sign rules when working with negative fractions.
Find a fraction of an amount and solve reverse problems.
Convert between fractions, decimals and percentages and use these links to compare quantities.
Solve multi-step word problems and check answers for reasonableness.
Apply the correct order of operations, including brackets, to calculations that mix fractions and decimals.

concepts.title: What a Fraction Really Means
concepts.explanation:
A fraction can be read in three connected ways, and a strong mathematician moves easily between them. Take 3/4. First, it is a part of a whole: 3 out of 4 equal parts, like 3 of the 4 quarters of an anjero. Second, it is a ratio: the relationship 3 to 4. Third, it is a division: 3 divided by 4, which equals 0.75. These are not three different fractions — they are three views of the same object, and being fluent in all three is what lets you attack any problem.

Every fraction has a numerator (the top, counting how many parts you have) and a denominator (the bottom, telling you how many equal parts make one whole). The bar between them literally means 'divided by'. When the numerator is smaller than the denominator, the fraction is proper and its value is less than 1. When the numerator is equal to or larger than the denominator, the fraction is improper and its value is 1 or more. A mixed number such as 2 3/4 is just another way of writing an improper fraction.

Why does the 'division' reading matter so much? Because it is the bridge to decimals and percentages, which you will meet in Concept 7. If a fraction is genuinely just a division waiting to happen, then 3/4 and '3 divided by 4' and 0.75 are all the same number wearing different clothes. Keeping this in mind stops fractions from feeling like a separate, mysterious topic — they are simply numbers, and every rule you already know about numbers still applies to them.

Converting between improper fractions and mixed numbers

To change a mixed number into an improper fraction, multiply the whole number by the denominator and add the numerator, keeping the same denominator. For example, 2 3/4 = (2 × 4 + 3)/4 = 11/4. To change an improper fraction back, divide the numerator by the denominator: the quotient is the whole number and the remainder becomes the new numerator. For example, 11/4 = 2 remainder 3 = 2 3/4. You will do this constantly when multiplying and dividing, so practise until it is automatic.

Equivalent fractions and simplifying
concepts.example: Equivalent fractions name the same value with different numbers. If you multiply or divide both the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number, the value does not change: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 5/10, and 3/4 = 6/8 = 9/12 = 75/100. To simplify a fraction, find the highest common factor (HCF) of the numerator and denominator and divide both by it. To simplify 24/36, the factors of 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24 and the factors of 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36, so the HCF is 12, and 24/36 = (24 ÷ 12)/(36 ÷ 12) = 2/3. Always give a final answer in simplest form.

concepts.title: Comparing and Ordering Fractions
concepts.explanation:
To compare fractions you must compare like with like. There are several reliable methods, and choosing the right one saves time.

Method 1 — Common denominators. Rewrite the fractions so they share a denominator, then compare numerators. To compare 2/3 and 3/4, the lowest common denominator of 3 and 4 is 12, so 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12. Since 8/12 < 9/12, we have 2/3 < 3/4. This method is the most reliable, especially when ordering three or more fractions.

Method 2 — Cross multiplication. To compare a/b and c/d, compare the products a × d and b × c. To compare 3/5 and 4/7, work out 3 × 7 = 21 and 5 × 4 = 20. Since 21 > 20, 3/5 > 4/7. This is quick for exactly two fractions.

Method 3 — Convert to decimals. Divide each fraction out. To compare 5/8 and 7/12, note 5/8 = 0.625 and 7/12 = 0.583…, so 5/8 > 7/12. This is handy when you also need the decimal value.

Method 4 — Benchmarks. Use familiar fractions such as 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4 as reference points to make a quick judgement before calculating precisely.
concepts.example: To order 2/3, 5/8, 3/4 and 7/12 from smallest to largest, use a common denominator. The LCM of 3, 8, 4 and 12 is 24, giving 2/3 = 16/24, 5/8 = 15/24, 3/4 = 18/24 and 7/12 = 14/24. Reading the numerators in order — 14, 15, 16, 18 — the answer is 7/12 < 5/8 < 2/3 < 3/4.

concepts.title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions
concepts.explanation:
You can only add or subtract fractions when they are cut into pieces of the same size — that is, when they share a denominator. With like denominators, simply add or subtract the numerators and keep the denominator: 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7, and 5/8 − 2/8 = 3/8. Always simplify the result: 7/9 − 4/9 = 3/9 = 1/3.

With unlike denominators, first find the lowest common denominator (LCD), rewrite each fraction as an equivalent fraction over that denominator, then add or subtract. For 1/4 + 1/6, the LCD of 4 and 6 is 12, so 1/4 = 3/12 and 1/6 = 2/12, giving 3/12 + 2/12 = 5/12. For 3/4 − 1/3, the LCD is 12, so 3/4 = 9/12 and 1/3 = 4/12, giving 9/12 − 4/12 = 5/12.

There are two good methods. Method A — parts separately: add the whole numbers, then add the fractions, then combine. For 2 1/4 + 1 5/8, the wholes give 2 + 1 = 3, and the fractions give 1/4 + 5/8 = 2/8 + 5/8 = 7/8, so the answer is 3 7/8. Method B — improper fractions: convert first, then work as usual. For 3 2/3 − 1 3/4, convert to 11/3 − 7/4; the LCD is 12, giving 44/12 − 21/12 = 23/12 = 1 11/12.

Sometimes the fraction you are subtracting is larger than the one you have. For 4 1/8 − 2 5/8 you cannot take 5/8 from 1/8, so borrow one whole from the 4: rewrite 4 1/8 as 3 + 1 + 1/8 = 3 9/8. Now subtract: 3 9/8 − 2 5/8 = 1 4/8 = 1 1/2. Borrowing with fractions works just like borrowing with column subtraction, except the 'one' you carry across is worth a whole denominator's worth of parts.

Adding and subtracting negative fractions
concepts.example: Two rules do all the work: adding a negative is the same as subtracting a positive, and subtracting a negative is the same as adding a positive. So 2/3 + (−1/4) = 2/3 − 1/4 = 8/12 − 3/12 = 5/12, and 1/2 − (−3/8) = 1/2 + 3/8 = 4/8 + 3/8 = 7/8. When both are negative, add the sizes and keep the negative sign: −2/5 + (−1/3) = −(6/15 + 5/15) = −11/15.

concepts.title: Multiplying Fractions
concepts.explanation:
Multiplying is the most forgiving of the four operations, because you do not need a common denominator. Simply multiply the numerators together and multiply the denominators together: a/b × c/d = (a × c)/(b × d). For example, 2/3 × 1/4 = 2/12 = 1/6, and 3/5 × 2/7 = 6/35.

Conceptually, multiplying fractions means taking a 'fraction of a fraction'. The calculation 1/2 × 3/4 means 'one half of three-quarters'. Start with 3/4 and take half of it, and you land on 3/8. This is why multiplying by a proper fraction (less than 1) makes a number smaller, which can feel surprising at first.

The opposite also holds, and it is worth pausing on. Multiplying by an improper fraction (greater than 1) makes a number larger, and multiplying by exactly 1 — in any disguise, such as 5/5 or 8/8 — leaves it unchanged. This last idea is secretly how equivalent fractions work: when you rewrite 2/3 as 8/12 you are really multiplying by 4/4, which equals 1, so the value never moves. Watching for hidden 'multiply by one' steps will make many later topics, including algebra, feel familiar rather than strange.

You can simplify before multiplying by cancelling a common factor from any numerator against any denominator. For 4/9 × 3/8, the 4 and the 8 share a factor of 4, and the 3 and the 9 share a factor of 3. Cancelling gives (1)/(3) × (1)/(2) = 1/6. Cross-cancelling keeps the numbers small, reduces mistakes, and leaves the answer already in simplest form.

Always convert mixed numbers to improper fractions first. For 2 1/4 × 1 2/3, convert to 9/4 × 5/3 = 45/12 = 15/4 = 3 3/4. To multiply by a whole number, write it over 1: 5 × 2/3 = 5/1 × 2/3 = 10/3 = 3 1/3. An area is a natural use: a rectangle 3 1/2 feet by 2 1/4 feet has area 7/2 × 9/4 = 63/8 = 7 7/8 square feet.
concepts.example: The sign rules are the same as for integers: positive × positive = positive; positive × negative = negative; negative × negative = positive. So 2/3 × (−1/4) = −1/6, while (−3/5) × (−2/7) = 6/35.

concepts.title: Dividing Fractions
concepts.explanation:
Why does flipping work? Division asks 'how many of these fit into that?'. The calculation 3/4 ÷ 1/8 means 'how many eighths are in three-quarters?'. Since 3/4 = 6/8, the answer is 6. Using the rule: 3/4 × 8/1 = 24/4 = 6. The two agree, which is exactly what we should expect.

For 2/3 ÷ 4/5: keep 2/3, change to ×, flip 4/5 to 5/4, then 2/3 × 5/4 = 10/12 = 5/6. For a whole number, 8 ÷ 2/3 = 8/1 × 3/2 = 24/2 = 12 — there are twelve two-thirds in 8. Notice that dividing by a fraction less than 1 makes the answer larger, because many small pieces fit into the whole.
concepts.example: Convert to improper fractions first. For 3 1/4 ÷ 1 2/3, convert to 13/4 ÷ 5/3 = 13/4 × 3/5 = 39/20 = 1 19/20. The sign rules for division are identical to those for multiplication, so 3/4 ÷ (−1/2) = 3/4 × (−2/1) = −6/4 = −3/2.

concepts.title: Fractions of an Amount
concepts.explanation:
Finding a fraction of an amount is a multiplication in disguise, and it appears constantly in real life. To find 3/5 of 40, either multiply directly — 3/5 × 40 = 120/5 = 24 — or use the two-step rule that many people find quicker: divide by the denominator, then multiply by the numerator. So 40 ÷ 5 = 8 (that is one-fifth), and 8 × 3 = 24 (that is three-fifths). Both give 24.

For example, Yusuf earns 3500 shillings helping at the market and gives 2/7 of it to help a neighbour. One-seventh is 3500 ÷ 7 = 500, so two-sevenths is 500 × 2 = 1000 shillings. Reverse problems run the method backwards. If 3/8 of a herd is 21 camels, then one-eighth is 21 ÷ 3 = 7, so the whole herd is 7 × 8 = 56 camels.
concepts.example: Yusuf earns 3500 shillings helping at the market and gives 2/7 of it to help a neighbour. One-seventh is 3500 ÷ 7 = 500, so 2/7 is 500 × 2 = 1000 shillings for the neighbour, leaving Yusuf with 3500 − 1000 = 2500 shillings for himself.

concepts.title: Order of Operations with Fractions and Decimals
concepts.explanation: The BIDMAS order of operations you used for integers — Brackets, Indices, Division and Multiplication (left to right), then Addition and Subtraction (left to right) — applies in exactly the same way when a calculation mixes fractions and decimals. Work out anything inside brackets first, then any powers or roots, then all multiplication and division from left to right, and finally all addition and subtraction from left to right. The only extra care needed is technical: convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing, and line up decimal points carefully before adding or subtracting. A common mistake is to work straight across in the order the numbers appear, instead of respecting brackets and the multiply/divide-before-add/subtract rule — this gives a wrong answer even though every individual fraction or decimal calculation was done correctly.
concepts.example: Evaluate (1/2 + 1/4) × 2/3, and then evaluate 0.6 + 0.4 × 5. Solution: For the first: brackets first, 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4; then multiply, 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2. For the second: multiplication before addition, 0.4 × 5 = 2.0; then add, 0.6 + 2.0 = 2.6. (Working left to right instead would wrongly give 0.6 + 0.4 = 1.0, then 1.0 × 5 = 5.0 — the wrong order changes the answer completely.)

methods.title: Fraction of an amount
methods.example: Find 2/5 of 45. Then, if 2/5 of a number is 30, find the original number.
steps: Divide the amount by the denominator to find one part.
Multiply that result by the numerator.
To find the whole from a part, divide by the numerator, then multiply by the denominator.

methods.title: Converting between forms
methods.example: Convert 5/8 to a decimal and then to a percentage.
steps: Fraction to decimal: divide numerator by denominator.
Decimal to percentage: multiply by 100. Percentage to decimal: divide by 100.
Fraction to percentage: convert to a decimal, then multiply by 100.

methods.title: Simplifying a fraction
steps: Find the highest common factor (HCF) of numerator and denominator.
Divide both by the HCF.
Check nothing but 1 divides both numbers now.

methods.title: Multiply with cross-cancelling
steps: Cancel 5 with 15 (both ÷ 5) and 4 with 8 (both ÷ 4): this gives 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6.
Cross-cancelling meant no large numbers and no simplifying at the end.
Check by multiplying the original fractions without cancelling — you should still get 1/6.

methods.title: Divide fractions
methods.example: Amina has 6 cups of flour and each batch of anjero needs 3/4 cup. How many batches can she make?
steps: This asks how many 3/4 fit into 6, so 6 ÷ 3/4 = 6/1 × 4/3 = 24/3 = 8 batches.
Keep the whole number, change ÷ to ×, and flip the fraction upside down.
Check by multiplying your answer by 3/4 — 8 × 3/4 should give back 6.

methods.title: Fraction of an amount and its reverse
methods.example: (a) Find 5/9 of 63 goats. (b) If 4/7 of a flock is 28 sheep, how big is the whole flock?
steps: (b) One-seventh is 28 ÷ 4 = 7, so the whole flock is 7 × 7 = 49 sheep.
Check part (a) by multiplying 5 × 7 to confirm 35, and part (b) by multiplying 7 × 7 to confirm 49.

workedExamples.title: Simplify a fraction
workedExamples.solution: The HCF of 42 and 56 is 14. Dividing both by 14 gives 42 ÷ 14 = 3 and 56 ÷ 14 = 4, so 42/56 = 3/4.

workedExamples.title: Order fractions
workedExamples.solution: The LCM of 6, 4 and 9 is 36. Convert: 5/6 = 30/36, 3/4 = 27/36, 7/9 = 28/36. Reading numerators 27, 28, 30 gives 3/4 < 7/9 < 5/6.

workedExamples.title: Subtract mixed numbers with borrowing
workedExamples.prompt: A plank is 8 5/8 inches long. Hassan cuts off 2 3/4 inches. What length remains?
workedExamples.solution: Write 3/4 as 6/8, so we need 8 5/8 − 2 6/8. Since 6/8 is larger than 5/8, borrow one whole: 8 5/8 = 7 13/8. Then 7 13/8 − 2 6/8 = 5 7/8. The plank has 5 7/8 inches left.

workedExamples.title: Multiply with cross-cancelling
workedExamples.solution: Cancel 5 with 15 (both ÷ 5) and 4 with 8 (both ÷ 4): this gives 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6. Cross-cancelling meant no large numbers and no simplifying at the end.

workedExamples.title: Divide fractions
workedExamples.prompt: Amina has 6 cups of flour and each batch of anjero needs 3/4 cup. How many batches can she make?
workedExamples.solution: This asks how many 3/4 fit into 6, so 6 ÷ 3/4 = 6/1 × 4/3 = 24/3 = 8 batches.

workedExamples.title: Fraction of an amount and its reverse
workedExamples.prompt: (a) Find 5/9 of 63 goats. (b) If 4/7 of a flock is 28 sheep, how big is the whole flock?
workedExamples.solution: (a) 63 ÷ 9 = 7, then 7 × 5 = 35 goats. (b) One-seventh is 28 ÷ 4 = 7, so the whole flock is 7 × 7 = 49 sheep.

workedExamples.title: Fraction–decimal–percentage comparison
workedExamples.solution: Convert to the same form: 7/8 = 0.875 = 87.5%. Since 87.5% > 85%, 7/8 is larger.

workedExamples.title: Negative fractions in context
workedExamples.prompt: One morning the temperature is −1 3/4°C and it rises by 3 1/2°C by midday. What is the midday temperature?

activities.title: The Kitchen Fraction Lab (Recipe Scaling)
activities.materials: a simple recipe (for anjero, bariis or a fruit salad), measuring cups or a clean container, and paper.
steps: Write out the ingredients of a recipe that serves 4 people.
Work out the scale factor to serve 10 people (10/4 = 5/2 = 2 1/2).
Multiply each ingredient by 2 1/2, converting any mixed numbers to improper fractions first.
If any answer is an improper fraction, convert it back to a mixed number so it is easy to measure.
Check one amount by estimating: does 'about two and a half times more' look right?

activities.title: The Measuring Tape Challenge (Adding and Subtracting)
activities.materials: a tape measure or ruler marked in fractions of an inch, and some objects to measure.
steps: Measure three objects to the nearest 1/8 inch and write each length as a mixed number.
Add two of the lengths together, finding a common denominator.
Find the difference between the longest and shortest object, borrowing if you need to.
Ask a family member to check your measurements and your arithmetic, or double-check your own working carefully (or ask your AI tutor) if nobody is available.

activities.title: Fraction War (A Comparing Game)
activities.materials: paper cards, each showing a fraction (mix easy and tricky denominators).
steps: Shuffle the cards and deal them equally between two players — if you do not have a partner, deal two hands to yourself or play against your AI tutor.
Each player turns over one card at the same time.
Whoever has the larger fraction wins both cards — use common denominators or decimals to decide.
If the fractions are equal, turn over another card to break the tie. Play until one player holds all the cards.
This game trains you to compare fractions quickly and to justify which is larger.

activities.title: The Discount Detective (Fractions, Decimals, Percentages)
activities.materials: a few price tags or made-up prices, and paper.
steps: Invent two shops selling the same item, one advertising a fraction off (say 3/8) and one a percentage off (say 35%).
Convert both discounts to percentages so they are in the same language.
Work out the final price in each shop.
Decide which shop is the better deal and explain your reasoning in one sentence.

activities.title: The Fair-Share Investigation
activities.materials: a bag of dates, beans or stones, and family members or friends to share with (or simply imagine a group size if nobody is available).
steps: Count out a number of dates that does not divide evenly among your group (for example 20 dates among 3 people).
Work out each person's share as a fraction and as a mixed number.
Now share 2/5 of the whole bag for charity: find the fraction of the amount.
Investigate: for which group sizes does the sharing come out exactly, and for which is there a fractional remainder? Record what you notice.

activities.title: Build a Fraction Wall
activities.materials: paper, a ruler, a pencil, and colours.
steps: Draw several equal-length bars stacked on top of each other.
Split the first into 1 part, the next into halves, then thirds, quarters, fifths, sixths, eighths, and so on.
Colour each row and label every piece with its fraction.
Use your wall to spot equivalent fractions (which pieces line up exactly?) and to compare sizes at a glance.
Keep your fraction wall — it is a powerful visual aid for the whole unit.

rules.title: The Division Reading of a Fraction
rules.text: Why does the 'division' reading matter so much? Because it is the bridge to decimals and percentages, which you will meet in Concept 7. If a fraction is genuinely just a division waiting to happen, then 3/4 and '3 divided by 4' and 0.75 are all the same number wearing different clothes. Keeping this in mind stops fractions from feeling like a separate, mysterious topic — they are simply numbers, and every rule you already know about numbers still applies to them.

rules.title: Why Dividing by a Fraction Means Flipping It
rules.text: Why does flipping work? Division asks 'how many of these fit into that?'. The calculation 3/4 ÷ 1/8 means 'how many eighths are in three-quarters?'. Since 3/4 = 6/8, the answer is 6. Using the rule: 3/4 × 8/1 = 24/4 = 6. The two agree, which is exactly what we should expect.

rules.title: The Divide-Then-Multiply Shortcut
rules.text: Finding a fraction of an amount is a multiplication in disguise, and it appears constantly in real life. To find 3/5 of 40, either multiply directly — 3/5 × 40 = 120/5 = 24 — or use the two-step rule that many people find quicker: divide by the denominator, then multiply by the numerator. So 40 ÷ 5 = 8 (that is one-fifth), and 8 × 3 = 24 (that is three-fifths). Both give 24.

questions.question: Convert 17/5 to a mixed number.
questions.hint: Divide the numerator by the denominator; the remainder becomes the new numerator.

questions.question: Simplify 18/24 to its lowest terms.
questions.hint: Find the highest common factor of the numerator and denominator, then divide both by it.
questions.explanation: The HCF of 18 and 24 is 6. Dividing both by 6 gives 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 24 ÷ 6 = 4, so 18/24 = 3/4.

questions.question: Which fraction is larger: 5/6 or 7/9?
questions.hint: Rewrite both fractions over a common denominator, then compare the numerators.
questions.explanation: The LCD of 6 and 9 is 18: 5/6 = 15/18 and 7/9 = 14/18. Since 15/18 > 14/18, 5/6 is larger.

questions.question: Work out 5 1/4 − 2 3/4.
questions.hint: You may need to borrow a whole one from the whole-number part before subtracting.
questions.explanation: Since 3/4 is bigger than 1/4, borrow one whole: 5 1/4 = 4 5/4. Then 4 5/4 − 2 3/4 = 2 2/4 = 2 1/2.

questions.question: Work out 5/8 × 4/15, giving your answer in simplest form.
questions.hint: Look for common factors between a numerator and a denominator before multiplying.
questions.explanation: Cancel 5 with 15 (both ÷ 5) and 4 with 8 (both ÷ 4): this gives 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6.

questions.question: Work out 5/8 ÷ 2/3.
questions.hint: Keep the first fraction, change the sign to ×, then flip the second fraction.
questions.explanation: Keep 5/8, change ÷ to ×, and flip 2/3 to 3/2: 5/8 × 3/2 = 15/16.

questions.question: Work out −3/4 × (−2/5).
questions.hint: Multiply the numbers first, then apply the sign rules for negatives.
questions.explanation: A negative multiplied by a negative gives a positive: 3/4 × 2/5 = 6/20 = 3/10.

questions.question: If 3/8 of a flock is 45 sheep, how many sheep are in the whole flock?
questions.hint: Find the value of one part first, then multiply up to the whole.
questions.explanation: One-eighth of the flock is 45 ÷ 3 = 15 sheep, so the whole flock is 15 × 8 = 120 sheep.

questions.question: Convert 4 2/5 to an improper fraction.
questions.hint: Multiply the whole number by the denominator, then add the numerator; keep the same denominator.
questions.explanation: Multiply the whole number by the denominator and add the numerator: (4 × 5) + 2 = 22, so 4 2/5 = 22/5.

selfAssessment: I can interpret a fraction as a part of a whole, a ratio, and a division, and convert freely between improper fractions and mixed numbers.
I can find equivalent fractions and simplify to lowest terms using the highest common factor.
I can compare and order fractions (including negative fractions) using common denominators, cross multiplication and decimals.
I can add and subtract fractions and mixed numbers with unlike denominators, including borrowing.
I can multiply fractions and mixed numbers, using cross-cancelling to simplify.
I can divide fractions and mixed numbers using the multiply-by-the-reciprocal method.
I can apply the correct sign rules when working with negative fractions.
I can find a fraction of an amount and solve reverse problems.
I can convert between fractions, decimals and percentages and use these links to compare quantities.
I can solve multi-step word problems and check answers for reasonableness.
